title: Canonical and Canonoid Transformations of Hamiltonian Systems on $q$-Cosymplectic and $q$-Contact Manifolds
authors: Giuseppe Marmo, Cristina Sard\'on, Xuefeng Zhao
abstract:
arXiv:2611.24961v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: $q$-Cosymplectic and $q$-contact structures equip presymplectic and precontact geometry with additional one-forms and a normalized family of Reeb vector fields. We study canonical and canonoid transformations relative to these data, with particular attention to their origin in constrained mechanical systems. In the $q$-cosymplectic and uniform $q$-contact cases, we establish local normal forms, characterize infinitesimal automorphisms, and obtain Noether-type relations between symmetries and conserved or dissipated quantities. For a one-parameter group of canonoid transformations with generator $X$, we show that $[X,X_H]$ is Hamiltonian and determine its Hamiltonian function. In the uniform $q$-contact case, simultaneous constant rescalings of the defining forms provide canonoid transformations for every Hamiltonian. The geometric constructions are illustrated by regular relativistic mass-shell constraints and by global Lagrangian descriptions of a charge in magnetic monopole fields. These examples distinguish parameters along constraint orbits from physical time and clarify the role of gauge directions. They also recover the total angular momentum of free relativistic particles and the Poincar\'e angular momentum of the charge--monopole system. For two monopoles, we construct a non-uniform $2$-contact structure and prove a topological obstruction to a uniform structure with the prescribed gauge generators as Reeb fields. Irrationally related magnetic charges additionally obstruct the intermediate quotient that would produce a single contact manifold. This example identifies a limitation of the uniform theory and motivates its extension to non-uniform structures.

title: Entanglement Geometry Beyond Polygons: Graph-Theoretic Entanglement Inequalities
authors: Masoud Gharahi
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25019v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Entanglement entropies of pure multipartite states can be constrained by organizing subsystem cuts as edges (hyperedges) of graphs (hypergraphs). Starting from the one-party entanglement polygon inequality, we derive these constraints from strong subadditivity and pure-state complementarity, with optimal coefficients and explicit equality conditions. Our central result determines, for a distinguished two-party cut and an arbitrary weighted family of cuts, the optimal polygon coefficient: the smallest total weight of the cuts separating a member of the distinguished pair from a remaining party. A refinement involving three mutual information terms gives the exact minimum of the weighted sum at fixed entropies of the two parties and of their union, attained by at most three independent bipartite pure states. This criterion recovers the cycle and complete-graph inequalities and shows that uniform incidence parity, which we prove sufficient for polygon inequalities on hypergraphs, is not necessary. Averaging strong subadditivity over both sides of a bipartition gives a sharp $k$-marginal inequality with coefficient $2\binom{n-2}{k-1}$, and we determine uniformly optimal coefficients for collective hyperstar inequalities. For paths and overlapping hyperchains, the deficits are exact sums of conditional mutual information terms; genuinely multipartite entangled cluster states saturate the hyperchain inequality while the chain inequality remains strict. We characterize pure chain equality states, bound the trace distance to cycle equality states independently of the number of parties and local dimensions, and obtain bond-dimension bounds for matrix product states and sequential-recovery error estimates.

title: The Clifford Hierarchy from Clifford Stabilizers in 2D
authors: Alison Warman, Sakura Schafer-Nameki
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25025v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The Bravyi-K\"onig theorem limits the constant-depth logical gates of 2D topological Pauli stabilizer codes to be in the Clifford group. Known qubit codes with Clifford stabilizers exceed it by only one level of the Clifford hierarchy, and this was conjectured to hold generally. We show that this bound can be completely bypassed, and that topological codes with Clifford stabilizers in 2D can realize transversal logical gates at any level of the Clifford hierarchy. We present two explicit constructions of codes based on copies of the quantum doubles of $D_4$ and $\mathbb{Z}_2$, with $k$ logical qubits and a logical $C^{k-1}Z$ gate, which is at level $k$ of the Clifford hierarchy. The physical circuits realizing the gates consist only of physical $Z$ or $CZ$ gates. The main new ingredient comes from the logical encoding, which depends crucially on non-Abelian group multiplication.

title: Passive memories beyond the Ising model: from SFQ to GKP
authors: Simon Lieu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25030v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-correcting quantum memories are spin Hamiltonians that aim to generalize the classical memory of the magnetic hard disk (i.e. ferromagnetic Ising model) to protect against both bit flips and phase flips. Beyond the magnetic hard disk, there are other passive classical memories that are used in modern computers, notably: the flash memory in laptops (which traps charge on a conducting island), and the flux storage loop in single-flux quantum (SFQ) logic (which traps flux in a superconducting loop). In this paper we review how storage and writing work in these two classical memories, drawing analogies to the charge qubit and the flux qubit. Protection in these systems derives not from scaling a lattice to the thermodynamic limit, but from a large, tunable energy barrier that separates codewords during memory, yet can be suppressed during a write. Towards protecting a qubit: We introduce a 2D ``floating XY model'' that combines the exponential (phase-flip) protection of the floating charge island with the polynomial (bit-flip) protection of the ferromagnetic XY model. We also study a self-dual superconducting circuit that hosts GKP codewords as symmetry-broken ground states of a $\mathbb{Z}_2 \times \mathbb{Z}_2 $-symmetric circuit, and discuss its protection and limitations.

title: Birthday-Scale Non-Adaptive Security for Strong Pseudorandom Unitaries
authors: Zvika Brakerski, Lior Ozer, Shahar Silberstein
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25038v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Pseudorandom unitaries (PRUs) are efficiently implementable unitary ensembles that are computationally indistinguishable from Haar-random unitaries, providing efficient substitutes for Haar-randomness in quantum information and cryptography. Strong PRUs require this indistinguishability to hold even when the adversary is given access to all of $U$, $U^\dagger$, $U^*$, and $U^T$.
  In this work, we prove birthday-scale non-adaptive security for the DPFC (Clifford-Phase-Permutation-Clifford) strong PRU candidate. For an $N$-dimensional unitary, allowing arbitrary entangled inputs and coherent superpositions of query types, we show that DPFC can withstand $t \approx \sqrt{N}$ queries. This matches the best known query complexity even for PRUs that are not strong, compared with $t \approx N^\alpha$ for $\alpha < 1/2$ in previous strong-PRU analyses.
  Our proof utilizes two techniques from previous works: the EPR-sector decomposition of Schuster et al. (arXiv 2025), previously used for unitary designs but not for PRUs, and the path-recording framework of Ma and Huang (STOC 2025), previously used for adaptive security analysis.
  We complement the non-adaptive security result with an upper bound in the adaptive setting, showing that DPFC cannot remain secure for $t \gg \sqrt{N}$ queries.

title: A Basis-Dependent Kernel for Learning Quantum Phases of Matter
authors: Clemens Lindner, Vin\'icius Mohr, Adri\'an P\'erez-Salinas
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25048v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Identifying the phases of a quantum many-body system as its parameters vary is a central problem in condensed-matter physics. Data-driven approaches address this task by comparing quantum states, for instance through their fidelity, and locating transitions where these comparisons change abruptly. In this work, we introduce the inverse participation ratio (IPR) kernel, a kernel method built for learning quantum phases of matter from IPRs in physically motivated bases. Unlike fidelity-based kernels, the IPR kernel can identify states with physically meaningful similarity even when they are orthogonal. We test the method on ground states of the transverse-field Ising (TFIM) and Heisenberg XXZ models. For TFIM Gibbs states, we further show that the IPR kernel retains phase-relevant structure over a range of nonzero temperatures where the phase signal of fidelity-based kernels is already degraded. More broadly, our results suggest that quantum kernels benefit more from feature maps tailored to the physics of the problem than from maximal expressivity.

title: Modeling couplings and quench dynamics of hundred-qubit quantum processors
authors: Simon Pettersson Fors, Eric Dj\"aknegren, Jorge Fern\'andez-Pend\'as, Anton Frisk Kockum
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25053v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum processors now operate beyond the reach of exact classical simulation, yet their design and verification rest on precise models of the device. Understanding which properties of quantum processors can still be predicted on classical computers is central both to building these machines and to delimiting claims of quantum advantage. Here we address this question at the device level, using continuous unitary transformations to derive effective Hamiltonians non-perturbatively for two-dimensional superconducting processors at a cost polynomial in qubit number. For a 96-transmon array with tunable couplers, we extract the effective qubit couplings, state-dependent interactions (e.g., ZZ couplings), and eigenstate locality that guide processor design. This computation parallelizes over tensor contractions and thus takes an hour at most per design point on a single GPU, enabling rapid design iterations of the full array. Combining these effective models with semiclassical sampling, we then predict the quench dynamics of 100 qubits and 180 couplers at half filling, a sector of dimension $10^{29}$, and validate the approach against exact dynamics of smaller arrays. We show that our approach captures relaxation, thermalization, and transport, but not the bitstring statistics underlying cross-entropy benchmarks. The predicted transport carries a fingerprint of the device: under a staggered detuning, excitations cross over from ballistic to diffusive spreading, slow down at a doublon resonance, and diffuse at different rates on each sublattice. Our results chart which observables lie within classical reach and offer a practical tool for designing future devices.

title: Certified Discovery of Quantum Phase Diagrams
authors: Yuanxi Liu, John Preskill, Hsin-Yuan Huang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25064v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Can a machine provably discover new quantum phases of matter? We show that the answer is yes under physically motivated assumptions. For any smooth family of geometrically local Hamiltonians, we construct an efficient quantum algorithm that outputs the phase diagram to prescribed accuracy and provides a verifiable certificate for every transition it reports. The algorithm takes as input only a classical description of the family together with unverified preparations of reference ground states; no order parameter, symmetry-breaking pattern, or training data are supplied. It succeeds provided that at least one preparation is correct in each gapped region of parameter space. The algorithm explores parameter space by quasi-adiabatically or adiabatically transporting each reference state, detecting the approach of a phase boundary by tapping the transported state with a frequency-filtered local probe: excitations created by the probe witness the closing of the energy gap. We prove that the gap closing for continuous phase transitions can always be detected using the frequency-filtered gradient of the Hamiltonian. The gap-detecting measurement is gentle, so when the ground state is unique a single reusable copy of each reference ground state supports the full exploration (for degenerate ground states, polynomially many copies suffice). The quantum algorithm runs in polynomial time at inverse-polynomial gap resolution. We also give a classical algorithm that runs in quasipolynomial time at constant gap resolution. Numerical experiments demonstrate how our algorithm accurately determines the phase structure of several model quantum systems.

title: Self-testing in Fermionic Networks
authors: Fatemeh Moradi Kalarde, Luis Mu\~{n}ecas Tom\'{a}s, Marc-Olivier Renou
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25074v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Self-testing certifies quantum states and measurements from observed correlations alone, without assumptions on the inner workings of the devices. Its standard formulation, however, models the devices as manipulating qudits, of arbitrary or even infinite dimension. Yet febits, information encoded in the presence or absence of a fermion in a mode, can produce correlations in quantum networks that no qudit model reproduces under the same locality constraints. We first show that the modeling choice in terms of qudits or febits matters for self-testing: some correlations that self-test a unique qudit strategy admit two fermionic realizations inequivalent under local parity-preserving isometries. We then develop a fermionic self-testing framework and show that the correlations of a three-party rewiring network single out febit states and measurements up to such isometries, providing the first genuine fermionic self-test.

title: On H\"older Equicontinuity of the Integrated Density of States for Random Schr\"odinger Operators on $\mathbb{Z}^d$
authors: Jan Fischer, David Hasler
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25077v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study a random Schr\"odinger operator $H_\lambda= H_0 + \lambda V$ on $\mathbb{Z}^d$ consisting of a translation invariant hopping matrix $H_0$ and a random potential $V$, given by independently distributed single site potentials with absolutely continuous distributions. Assuming a regularity assumption for the hopping matrix $H_0$, we show H\"older continuity of the integrated density of states of $H_\lambda$ up to exponents $2/3$, independently of the disorder strength $\lambda$.

title: A measurement-free quantum error correction protocol for superconducting cavities
authors: Q. Rumman Rahman, S. M. Girvin, D. K. Weiss
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25095v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The realization of large-scale quantum computation will require quantum error correction (QEC). One way to reduce the demands placed on QEC is to correct dominant physical errors at a lower level before passing the remaining errors to an outer code. Recently, Krastanov et al. [Nat. Commun. 12, 191 (2021)] proposed a measurement-free error-correction protocol based on coherent control of photonic modes that corrects for photon loss. Here, we adapt this approach to a circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED) architecture using three superconducting microwave cavities coupled by Josephson-junction-based nonlinear elements. We encode the logical qubit in the lowest-order binomial code of one cavity, while the two other cavities serve as ancillas. Using numerical simulations with experimentally realistic parameters, we demonstrate that our protocol can correct single-photon loss with 99% fidelity. Furthermore, we optimize the waiting time between successive rounds of error-correction, and show that the logical lifetime can be extended by a factor of 1.2-1.8 relative to the unprotected Fock $\{|0\rangle, |1\rangle\}$ encoding, surpassing break-even performance. Our work highlights the potential of gate-based, measurement-free QEC for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Agentic MLIR-to-QIR Translation with Dual-Backend Testing: A Hybrid Deterministic and LLM Approach
authors: Sharmin Afrose, Vicente Leyton-Ortega, Narasinga Rao Miniskar, Elaine Wong, Travis S. Humble
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25106v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum frameworks each define their own Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect, so porting a circuit to a Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR) runtime needs a hand-written pass per dialect. Our translator selects among three paths: a deterministic compiler path for known grammars (Catalyst and Quake), a large language model (LLM) agentic path for unseen dialects, and a repair path invoked when deterministic output fails testing. A dual-backend pipeline executes the source MLIR and generated QIR on independent simulators, comparing output distributions by total variation distance (TVD). For smaller open-weight models we replace retrieval-augmented generation with inline context engineering and add a guardrail-assembler that rebuilds valid QIR from incomplete output. Across 41 circuits spanning three dialects and 1-100 qubits, the deterministic path is gate-exact on all 70 circuit-dialect pairs, averaging above 95% TVD similarity (1-TVD). On an unseen fault-tolerant (FTQC) dialect, four of six models produce valid logical-level QIR on the first iteration.

title: Generalizing and Combining Check Constructions: Design-Space Exploration for Fault-Tolerant Quantum State Preparation
authors: Ludwig Schmid, Robert Wille
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25107v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing needs logical states prepared such that single faults cannot spread into uncorrectable errors. Post-selection achieves this with added checks that detect dangerous faults and discard the run. How the checks are measured sets the depth and operation count of the circuit, and the best trade-off depends on the hardware. Existing automated methods, however, each use one check construction and yield fixed trade-offs.
  We first introduce Block Checks, in which several checks share one fault-tolerantly prepared auxiliary block, which places them and existing constructions in a single design space. Second, to explore that space, we propose a Pareto tree search that adds checks and auxiliary blocks, merges auxiliaries, and edits the circuit. On quantum codes of distance up to seven, the search finds best-known circuits for many new operation--depth trade-offs and surpasses existing methods. The code is open source as part of the Munich Quantum Toolkit (MQT) at https://github.com/munich-quantum-toolkit/qecc, and all circuits are available in the QECirc library at https://qecirc.com.

title: A Computational and Experimental Framework for Fourier Optics in Python
authors: Rachel Migdal, Antoine Islegen-Wojdyla
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25116v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Simulation of the propagation of light is useful for the design and dimensioning of optical systems. In this paper, we present the basics of propagation simulation using Fourier optics and practical implementation in Python, with a particular emphasis on dimensions. We first verify that our numerical wave-optics simulations maintain correct physical spatial scaling. Next, we benchmark numerical propagation against closed-form analytical formulas for Gaussian beams, lens focusing effects, and grating diffraction. We then show how those simulations can be used to generate diffractive optical elements such as Fresnel zone plates, and we bridge the gap between numerical simulations and experiments by collecting data and recovering phase information using a phase retrieval algorithm.

title: A Quantum Continuous Wavelet Transform
authors: Brani Vidakovic
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25117v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We construct a quantum continuous wavelet transform (QCWT) on a finite scale--translation grid whose scales may be non-dyadic. A quantum Fourier transform places the amplitude-encoded signal in the frequency basis, the scale-dependent multiplier is block-encoded with one flag qubit, and an inverse Fourier transform returns the complex, quadrature-weighted CWT coefficients in the success branch. For heralded circuits that act once on one copy of the input with an input-independent output factor, we bound the success probability and attain the bound by a frequency-conditioned scale preparation. When the scale prior is prepared independently of frequency, normalizing the multiplier separately at each scale is optimal and raises the success probability by factors of 4.9 and 14.6 in our examples; on logarithmic grids this architecture loses, relative to the bound, a factor of about the admissibility constant over the squared spectral peak times the logarithmic scale range. We give a fixed-point resource estimate for a reversible Mexican-hat multiplier, the multinomial law of scale--translation measurements, and Hadamard tests for complex coefficients. We show that a Fourier-basis measurement of the input, followed by classical randomization, reproduces the flag and scale outcomes of every such heralded circuit exactly, so it is at least as informative for global scale energies; a simulation study of Hurst exponent estimation agrees. What the QCWT adds is the joint scale--translation law: two chirps with identical Fourier-basis and time-basis measurement laws have QCWT laws at total-variation distance 0.27.

title: Learning Integer Winding Evolution Times in Quantum Phase Estimation
authors: Elijah Pelofske, Stephan Eidenbenz
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25124v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Learning a Hamiltonian evolution time in Quantum Phase Estimation that produces phase distributions with low Shannon entropy circumvents the fundamental limit of digitization error of phase, independent of the number of phase qubits of accuracy. By introducing an optimization loop to minimize the Shannon entropy of measured eigenvalues produced by a QPE quantum circuit, minimum eigenvalue computation accuracy is greatly improved, which we show numerically on quantum magnet models. This technique works because standard QPE has a natural correspondence between entropy of the phase distribution and the analog accuracy of the minimum eigenvalue phase. This introduces for the first time a type of parameter learning to QPE, which makes near term practicality of QPE for fundamental sciences more feasible by using shorter depth QPE circuits.

title: Characterizing a neutral atom quantum simulator accessible in cloud
authors: Andrea Muratori, Francesco Minardi, Tommaso Calarco, Felix Motzoi
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25131v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Quantum simulators have become a reality in recent years, with several platforms now remotely accessible through the cloud. These systems give researchers the opportunity to run quantum programs without requiring either a dedicated laboratory or extensive experimental expertise, and, in several cases, they have already enabled the execution of relevant protocols with remarkable results. However, despite the impressive progress in the performance of these machines, they still suffer from various noise sources, some of which are not always completely clear to the end user, which limits their applicability to tasks that are sufficiently robust against noise of various kinds. In this work, we investigate the behavior of Fresnel, a remotely accessible neutral-atom analog quantum simulator provided by Pasqal. We design and perform a series of experiments probing the machine's response to various pulse sequences and experimental settings, and identify the main noise sources affecting its dynamics. Based on these data, we construct an effective model of the system's noisy evolution and use numerical optimization to infer the noise strengths. The resulting model accurately reproduces the simulator's dynamics, showing how effective noise models can be built for cloud-based quantum resources.

title: Accelerating Diffusion Maps on a Quantum Computer: Spectral Filtering and Galerkin PDE Solvers
authors: Ruizhe Qian, Xiantao Li
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25147v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Diffusion maps generalize principal component analysis (PCA) to nonlinear manifolds, enabling spectral dimensionality reduction, geometric data analysis, and elliptic PDE approximation on point clouds. For large datasets of size $N$, however, classical matrix operations incur prohibitive $\operatorname{poly}(N)$ scaling, even when extracting low-dimensional spectral features or targeted scalar observables. We introduce a quantum algorithmic framework that bypasses explicit graph-Laplacian assembly by exploiting the symmetric factorization $G = A^T A$ directly at the block-encoding level. Combining Gaussian moment dilation, Laplace-weighted linear combinations of unitaries (LCU), and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT), we implement spectral filters of $A$ to estimate heat-semigroup overlaps, regularized inverse queries, and energy responses, as well as to prepare spectral Galerkin solution states. A common-state construction further allows the block-encoding queries to be used across multiple scalar observables. Under polylogarithmic-cost block-encoding access to $A$ and state-preparation oracles, our heat-overlap algorithm achieves $O(\operatorname{polylog} N)$ gate complexity at fixed normalized precision, confidence, and spectral scale. Ideal statevector simulations validate our discrete circuit constructions, while a matched approximate-counting benchmark demonstrates the quadratic precision advantage of coherent amplitude estimation for energy readout.

title: Nodal Knotted Finite-Energy Spatiotemporally Localized Scalar Wave Solutions
authors: Ioannis M. Besieris, Peeter Saari
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25155v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Significant amount of information is available in wave optics about monochromatic paraxial beams characterized by nodal knots, the latter being threads of complete darkness (lines of zero intensity) tied into knots. Also, well -known are finite-energy spatiotemporally localized vector-valued wave solutions characterized by knotted to-pologies. Unfortunately, except for solutions to the Schr\"odinger-like equation describing anomalous dispersion, no scalar-valued spatiotemporally localized waves with analogous knotted topological structures are known to date. It is the goal in this article to fill in this gap by deriving finite-energy spatiotemporally localized scalar-valued wave solutions characterized specifically by Hopf and trefoil nodal knot topologies. This will extend to spatiotemporally localized pulsed fields the diverse important applications of mono-chromatic light beams, having nontrivial topological structures, in trapping and guiding particles, image processing and optical communications; also, in applications to biology and medicine.

title: A universal modal-noise limit for multimode photonic systems
authors: Kalaga Madhav
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25156v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Modal noise limits the photometric and spectroscopic stability of every multimode-to-single-mode photonic system, yet it is quantified device by device. For isotropic modal excitation at fixed input power, the fractional power fluctuation of any linear multimode system is shown to be fixed by one number: the participation ratio M_eff of the eigenvalues of K = T{\dag}WT. Monte Carlo for spatially filtered fibres, lossy lanterns, and integrated mode converters confirms the law, which recovers the classical speckle limits. Extending K to K({\lambda}) gives the spectral correlation of modal noise and a closed-form velocity error, maximal when the correlation width equals the line width.

title: The Complete Set of Solutions for the Equations of Temporal Coupled Mode Theory
authors: Matthew Beutel, Ming Zhou, Shanhui Fan
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25181v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Temporal coupled mode theory (TCMT) provides a compact description of resonant transport in optical systems in terms of a small set of physically transparent parameters, including the resonant coupling coefficients and direct background scattering matrix. In the formalism of TCMT, the background scattering matrix and the coupling vectors are constrained by time reversal symmetry, reciprocity, and energy conservation. While these constraints are well established, the general so- lution under these is only known for a few cases, in which spatial symmetry simplifies the problem. In this paper, we derive the complete set of solutions for the equations of temporal coupled mode theory that describes lossless single-mode or multi-mode resonators coupled to an arbitrary num- ber of ports. Our derivation utilizes an explicit Takagi decomposition of the symmetric unitary background scattering matrix. We provide a comparison with numerical simulations for both the single and multimode cases.

title: Analytic and Numerical Investigation of a Proposed Non-linear Extension of Quantum Mechanics
authors: Alan Chodos, Anastasiia Purtova
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25188v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this paper, additional properties of a previously introduced non-linear extension of quantum mechanics are investigated. Analytically, we uncover a limit in which the model reduces to ordinary linear quantum mechanics. We also perform a perturbation analysis about an exact solution studied in earlier work. The equations represent a system that is subject to a periodic driver, and we use Floquet theory to help determine its properties. Numerically, we compare the exact solution to the analytic approximation, and we exhibit several examples of how the non-linear effects influence particle trajectories, with particular emphasis on trajectories near the linear limit.

title: Tunable source of entangled microwaves by nonlinear scattering of magnons
authors: Marco Br\"uhlmann, Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25207v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We propose a route to prepare entangled states of microwaves propagating in spatially separated transmission lines using the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics of ferromagnetic spin waves (magnons). We first show that a driven magnon mode can produce entangled magnon pairs at low temperatures by spontaneous parametric down-conversion enabled by three-magnon processes. The anisotropic magnon properties in thin films result in strict phase-matching conditions which allow only a well-defined pair of magnon modes to be amplified. This mode selectivity allows to out-couple each amplified mode to an independent microwave transmission line, producing non-degenerate propagating microwave entanglement with current experimental parameters. In addition, we prove that the frequency difference between the two entangled microwaves can be dynamically tuned across a few-GHz range by changing the orientation of a bias magnetic field. Our figures of merit - .g., the amount of microwave entanglement - can be largely improved by optimizing material and geometry. Our work establishes that quantum states of propagating magnons can be created by their nonlinear dynamics alone, and opens a pathway toward integrating magnons in hybrid quantum platforms.

title: Certified Separation Between Coherent and Adaptive Temporal Processing of Quantum-Error-Correction Readout
authors: Shreya Savadatti, Matthew Reynolds, Jonathan Maack, Wesley Jones, Franz Franchetti
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25216v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Repeated quantum-error-correction readout is normally converted into a classical time series: each syndrome pulse is measured on arrival and only the resulting classical record is retained. Nonorthogonal readout signals raise the question of whether preserving quantum information between rounds can improve the final recovery decision. We formulate this comparison as a loss-weighted state-discrimination problem. For an idealized two-round benchmark with quadrature phase-shift-keying (QPSK) signals, a receiver with a seven-dimensional persistent register has certified recovery-decision error below $24.2100\%$, whereas every separate adaptive receiver has error above $25.1431\%$. The certified separation is at least $0.933$ percentage points. The loss counts incorrect final error-mask decisions in the benchmark. In the strict architecture, where the counted register is the entire persistent state, four dimensions are necessary and sufficient to outperform the adaptive class. Certified separations also occur at three and four rounds with register dimensions $8$ and $36$, compared with $16$ and $64$ for full-prefix storage. We relate memory dimension to the structure of the temporal measurement, give a sufficient memory bound for collective measurements, and quantify robustness to register dephasing and accumulated channel error.

title: Interacting framework for the free magnetic dynamics
authors: Giuseppe De Nittis
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25285v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: This is the second paper of a program aimed at a rigorous many--body theory of continuum fermions in a uniform magnetic field, built on the asymptotic quasi--local structure that the magnetic coherent--state frame induces on the CAR algebra. Here we study the free dynamics. We show that a Bogoliubov dynamics preserves the local structure exactly if and only if it is generated by a function of the Landau Hamiltonian. For this class we compute the hopping coefficients in closed form, prove that the Lieb--Robinson velocity vanishes, and determine when the almost--local algebra lies in the domain of the generator. For the Landau Hamiltonian the dynamics turns out to be periodic. We then describe the ground states and the KMS states at every temperature, prove their ergodicity under magnetic translations, and recover the KMS states at positive temperature as thermodynamic limits of local Gibbs states. Finally, we relate the exact hopping operator to the Hofstadter model. These results confirm that the frame--induced local structure is a consistent setting for the perturbed and interacting magnetic dynamics to be studied next.

title: Resilience of emergent Hamiltonian quantum memories in the presence of noise
authors: Anubhab Sur, Rubem Mondaini
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25286v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Emergent Hamiltonians can freeze an entangled state prepared through coherent evolution, since that state is an eigenstate of the Hamiltonian under which it is then stored. We show that the freedom left in this construction allows the storage spectrum to be adapted to a noisy environment without changing the stored state. For a product of Bell pairs prepared from a density wave in an engineered chain, a selection rule prevents local density noise from connecting the target to any of its degenerate partners, so that rescaling the storage Hamiltonian by a factor $\alpha$ moves every transition this noise drives. Under $1/f$ noise, the storage time then grows in proportion to $\alpha$, a result we confirm by evolving the memory under explicit classical $1/f$ fields, whereas for an Ohmic bath the most favorable scale depends on its cutoff. Fermionic loss, treated as a solvable model, includes a transition that rescaling leaves at zero frequency, and an energy shift $\mu$ per particle moves it away from zero, with an exact orbital solution giving the resulting lifetimes. Finally, among number-conserving quadratic reference Hamiltonians, $\alpha$ and $\mu$ are the only controls that keep the storage Hamiltonian nearest neighbor at every time along the preparation, so that the protocol combines local freezing with control over the storage spectrum.

title: Quantum dynamical transitions when the corresponding classical phase space has a separatrix: extension of the QKNH theorem beyond double wells
authors: Peter Stabel, James R. Anglin
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25299v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In classical Hamiltonian systems with a slowly time-dependent parameter, adiabaticity breaks down at a separatrix, leading to probabilistic post-adiabatic transitions between different phase-space regions described by the Kruskal-Neishtadt-Henrard (KNH) theorem. Quantum mechanically, dynamical tunneling allows adiabaticity to persist where it breaks down classically, making the quantum-classical correspondence for separatrix crossing non-trivial. We recently established a quantum version of the KNH theorem (QKNH) by introducing the concept of a sweep-rate-dependent quantum separatrix in the instantaneous energy spectrum of the time-dependent system. The QKNH theorem relates the splitting of a quantum ensemble between the outgoing dynamical sectors at the quantum separatrix to their relative growth rates, and thus provides a quantum analog of the classical KNH rule. Here, we demonstrate that these findings are not restricted to double-well systems with tunneling through a potential barrier. We investigate a slowly driven quantum pendulum, in which the avoided crossings arise from above-barrier reflection. The resulting Landau-Zener probabilities have the same local lattice form as in the double-well problem, allowing the application of the QKNH theorem.

title: Painlev\'e transcendents in the defocusing Hirota equation with non-zero boundary conditions
authors: Shuning Lin, Engui Fan

title: Generation of coherent-state Schr\"{o}dinger cat states in a two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model implemented with Josephson junctions
authors: Hiroo Azuma, William J. Munro, Kae Nemoto
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25323v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We investigate the generation of coherent-state Schr\"{o}dinger cat states using a two-photon Jaynes-Cummings model (JCM) implemented in a Josephson-junction quantum circuit. We consider a specific superconducting flux-qubit implementation and estimate the resulting two-photon coupling constant. We numerically examine three types of noise: magnetic flux noise with $1/f$ fluctuations, energy relaxation associated with the flux-qubit $T_{1}$ decay, and photon loss in the bosonic mode obtained by quantizing the phase variable of the dc SQUID used for qubit readout. We find that photon loss has a particularly significant effect on cat-state fidelity. We also investigate the time evolution of the probability-amplitude distribution in the Pegg-Barnett phase-state basis for the $l$-photon JCM ($l=1,2,3,4$), starting from a coherent bosonic state. Finally, we assume that the bosonic mode is initially prepared in a displaced thermal state and then decoupled from the heat bath. We study the subsequent unitary evolution to determine how the initial temperature affects the fidelity and Wigner function of the generated cat states.

title: Curvature-Calibrated Friction and an Exact Gauge Symmetry for Quantum Hamiltonian Descent
authors: Kentaro Hoshisashi
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25341v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: A design problem constrained by a partial differential equation can be solved coherently on a quantum computer. The objective is block-encoded rather than measured, and Quantum Hamiltonian Descent consumes it directly. We identify two obstacles in this pipeline and repair both. First, the oracle construction assumes affine generators with positive semidefinite Hermitian parts, which covariance entries violate for every off-diagonal generator. Encoding the covariance as an affine combination of positive semidefinite atoms restores both conditions at every register point, at the price of a representational floor, median 45% of the fitted family's own objective range for a fixed rank-three dictionary and 22% with a variable diagonal. Second, adding a constant to the objective leaves the measurement distribution exactly invariant, yet the mean-objective friction heuristic in current use assigns such objectives different schedules. Calibrating the friction to the landscape curvature restores the symmetry, though not the constant in $\nu = c\sqrt{\mu}$, and a bracketed sweep at matched objective-phase exposure, not end-to-end cost, places the best tested friction between 0.032 and 0.25 of critical damping on a diffusion-design benchmark, a broad plateau an order of magnitude below the classical default.

title: Semiclassical Averaging and Temporal Fluctuations of Quantum Dark Solitons in the Lieb-Liniger Model
authors: Kota Kaneko, Kohei Motegi, Jun Sato
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25343v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the time evolution of quantum dark-soliton states of the Lieb--Liniger model, introduced by Sato--Kanamoto--Kaminishi--Deguchi as equal-weight superpositions of one-hole yrast states, and their relation to Gross--Pitaevskii (GP) solitons. We consider a simultaneous weak-coupling and large-system limit in which the repulsive coupling constant $c$ tends to zero and the particle number $N$ and ring circumference $L$ tend to infinity, with the mean density $\bar n=N/L$ and scaled circumference $\Lambda=L\sqrt{c\bar n}$ fixed. We conjecture that, in this limit, the normalized quantum density and its evolution at fixed scaled time $\tau=c\bar n t$ are described by a canonical-momentum average of normalized periodic one-soliton GP densities, each evolving at its own velocity. We explicitly parametrize the GP family by canonical momentum and provide numerical evidence for this correspondence. The different velocities explain the spreading of the averaged density notch despite shape preservation by individual solitons. In the infinite-line limit, we derive an analytic expression for the initial averaged profile, establish an inverse-fifth-power decay of its density deficit with distance from the soliton center, and express the Fourier transform of its deviation from the background as a series of Bickley--Naylor functions $\operatorname{Ki}_3$. Following the spreading of the initial notch, we investigate temporal density fluctuations of the quantum dark solitons and propose a relation between long-time mode variances and second moments of GP Fourier coefficients, supported by numerical comparisons of individual mode variances and the total variance. Yrast transition frequencies distinguish the initial dephasing time scale from the longer scale associated with finite-time averaging of fluctuations.

title: Ising-Encoded Computational Homogenization: Stress as a Quantum Observable
authors: Mourad Halla, Suvranu De
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25383v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Computational homogenization requires repeated solutions of representative volume element (RVE) problems to determine the effective response transferred to the macroscale, including the homogenized stress. Here, we develop a basis-encoded, energy-based variational quantum formulation for linear-elastic computational homogenization. The reduced finite-element energy of the RVE is expressed as a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) problem and mapped to an Ising Hamiltonian, whose ground state represents the equilibrium fluctuation field on the encoding grid. Using the Hellmann--Feynman theorem, differentiation of the strain-dependent Hamiltonian with respect to the prescribed macroscopic strain yields stress observables whose expectation values recover the conventional volume-averaged homogenized stress. A key structural result is that, although the equilibrium Hamiltonian is two-local, the stress observables are one-local. In linear elasticity, the two-qubit coupling coefficients are independent of macroscopic strain, hence, differentiation eliminates all two-qubit coupling terms, leaving only identity and single-qubit Pauli-$Z$ operators. These observables are diagonal in the same computational basis as the Ising Hamiltonian and can therefore be evaluated from the same computational-basis measurements used for the energy. Consequently, the homogenized stress can be obtained directly from the optimized quantum state using the same computational basis measurements as the Ising Hamiltonian, without requiring reconstruction of the microscopic displacement field or an additional measurement basis. Ground states are approximated using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), and the formulation is demonstrated on a two-dimensional periodic RVE.

title: Counterfactual attribution of surface-code failures under non-Pauli noise: dependence on trajectory pairing
authors: Kisung Jin, Gyuil Cha
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25397v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Under Pauli noise in a stabilizer memory, attributing a quantum error-correction failure to the noise that caused it has a canonical answer; under non-Pauli noise the attribution depends on how trajectories are paired with their counterfactuals. We define a failing shot's cause set, the sites whose removal alone removes the failure, and separate it from pairing-independent net effects. The pairing enters wherever a fixed random draw meets a Born probability; making it maximal at every random step selects shared random numbers, while continuity does not. In a distance-three surface code, exact non-Pauli noise and its Pauli twirl fail at rates equivalent within a registered margin, yet under shared draws 20.2% of exact-noise failures need three or more sites, against 2.3% under the twirl. Other admissible pairings move the mean coherent cause count from 1.61 to 80 times the minimum the marginals allow, yet pairing-independent quantities barely separate the two models. Shot-level attributions should therefore state their pairing and report pairing-independent effects alongside.

title: AI-Native Industrial Control Systems: An Agent Architecture for the Control System Lifecycle
authors: Lisi Liu, Ang Zhou, Chuan Pang, Feng Gao, Shengkai Liu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25411v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Industrial control systems increasingly use AI for perception, control, and engineering, while available control functions and execution environments are typically established in advance. This paper proposes an AI-native industrial control system in which collaborating agents determine the capabilities required by a task, construct the control application, and prepare its execution environment. System-level agents coordinate device-level agents within configured resource and permission constraints. A physical sorting workstation illustrates two forms of adaptation. In the first case, controller and robot agents construct a sorting application on a prescribed Raspberry Pi target. In the second, a camera agent adds inspection on an edge node, and the controller associates inspection results with downstream pickup decisions. A subsequent revision enables selective sorting using the same agents and deployment arrangement. The trials demonstrate the feasibility of task-driven construction and evolution on the workstation. Commissioning also reveals limitations in the traceability of design decisions, adherence to delegated responsibilities, diagnostic reasoning, and verification of physical behavior.

title: High-Dimensional Structured Light Tomography with a Tilted Lens
authors: Altilano C. Barbosa, Isaac Tribaldo, Amanda K. Fritsch, Marcos G. de Oliveira, Gabriel Molina-Terriza, Antonio Z. Khoury
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25427v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In this work, we investigate high-dimensional spatial mode tomography using intensity measurements and the astigmatic transformation implemented with a tilted lens. We improve the method previously published in Ref. [1] to perform the spatial tomography not restricted to a fixed order, which allowed us to achieve good fidelity for a mode space dimension as high as $D=66\,$. Since the literature is not unanimous, we also present a comprehensive revision of light propagation through a tilted lens for an accurate description of the transformation used for tomography. We derive its effective focal lengths, and analyze its role as an astigmatic mode converter. Moreover, we establish its explicit domain of validity within the Hermite-Gaussian basis.

title: Interfacing Silicon Nitride Nanophotonics with Cuprous Oxide Rydberg Excitons
authors: Artem Kryvobok, Hamza Ather, Julio Herreros Garc\'ia, Ziqi Niu, Abhishek Bharatbhai Solanki, Vahagn Mkhitaryan, Benjamin Cerjan, Alexandra Boltasseva, Vladimir M. Shalaev, Hadiseh Alaeian
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25431v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Rydberg excitons in cuprous oxide (Cu$_2$O), the solid-state counterpart of Rydberg atoms, are hydrogen-like electron--hole quasi-particles with micron-sized wavefunctions and strong long-range interactions that promise optical nonlinearities at the few-photon level. Exploiting them in a waveguide quantum electrodynamics (WQED) setting can enable what atomic Rydberg platforms achieve only with ultrahigh vacuum and laser cooling/trapping---a guided optical mode interfaced with the Rydberg medium---while adding the scalability and advanced fabrication of integrated photonics. Here we demonstrate a monolithic, CMOS-compatible interface of Cu$_2$O Rydberg excitons with a SiN$_x$ nanophotonic waveguide. Under non-resonant excitation, excitonic emission from the Cu$_2$O microcrystal is coupled to the guided mode, routed along the waveguide, and collected from an output grating. The spectrum shows the phonon-assisted 1$s$ orthoexciton emission together with the low-lying 2$p$ and 3$p$ lines of the yellow Rydberg series. Spatially selective excitation excludes substrate background and direct scatter, and the enhanced linear polarization of the grating-collected signal identifies the TE-like guided mode as the collection channel. These results establish the complete material--device--measurement stack for a novel platform of nonlinear quantum nanophotonics based on Rydberg excitons.

title: A fast and accurate model for gradient-based inverse design of multimode waveguides
authors: Yuanze Chen, Zheng-Hua Chen, Yan-Xiao Gong, Shi-Ning Zhu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25432v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multimode photonic inverse design requires fast, accurate computational models that provide geometry gradients. Based on coupled-mode theory (CMT), we propose a differentiable surrogate model. Its parameter-extraction method uses a change of modal basis to obtain coupled-mode parameters from cross-sectional mode data. We also provide a complete, easy-to-implement propagation and optimization workflow. Using finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulation data as a common reference, we compare the prediction accuracy of our model and forward dataset-based eigenmode expansion (EME) for randomly generated thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN) waveguide profiles that traverse modal coupling regions. Using identical modal libraries, the model reduces the maximum per-mode mean absolute transmission error by 17-37% compared with forward EME. We demonstrate a spot-size converter design that preserves the fundamental TM$_0$ mode in its hybridization region with the first-order TE$_1$ mode and obtain nine structures, each with FDTD-verified transmission above 98%. These tests demonstrate the model's utility for large-scale photonic inverse design, enabling rapid exploration of the design parameter space by combining gradient information with improved prediction accuracy.

title: A Fa\`a di Bruno Convolution Identity in Parafermion Operator Products
authors: Sam Kault
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25455v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We give a detailed combinatorial proof of a Fa\`a di Bruno convolution identity used in parafermion operator-product calculations. The identity establishes the cancellation of potentially more singular terms and shows that the leading contribution combines the polynomial indices additively. The proof, originating in the author's doctoral thesis, provides a general derivation of an identity stated in earlier parafermion literature.

title: Dynamical Variational Theory of Stochastic Reaction Networks
authors: Moshir Harsh, Peter Sollich
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25491v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Discrete stochastic population dynamics describe systems ranging from biochemical reaction networks and gene regulation to epidemic spreading, ecology, and population genetics, where finite populations generate strong intrinsic fluctuations. Predicting their dynamics, including mean populations, fluctuations, time-lagged correlations, response functions, and steady states, remains challenging: the chemical master equation admits no general analytical solution, numerical solutions scale poorly with system size, and standard approximations fail at low copy numbers. Using a field-theoretic representation of the reaction dynamics, we develop a dynamical variational approximation for stochastic reaction networks based on the Plefka expansion from spin-glass physics. For reaction systems with general stoichiometry and time-dependent rates, the expansion yields tractable non-Markovian effective dynamics with self-consistent memory. We further introduce a generalized self-consistent bubble resummation that provides closed predictions for means, correlations, and response functions. The formulation applies broadly to discrete stochastic population dynamics on networks, and we provide a numerical implementation with adaptive time stepping for user-defined systems. We benchmark the method on stochastic gene regulation, enzyme kinetics, and infection dynamics, where it accurately captures both time-dependent behaviour and steady states, including fluctuation-driven effects missed by conventional approximations. Together, these results establish a general analytical framework for stochastic reaction dynamics across transient and stationary regimes in strongly fluctuating low-copy-number systems.

title: Convex splitting by binary quantum hypothesis testing
authors: Mark M. Wilde
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25496v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: How many independent quantum systems does it take to hide one system that is correlated with a reference? An observer can measure all the systems together with the reference to detect the correlation. We turn any such measurement into binary tests on a single system and the reference. For each test we bound the probability of declaring a signal when an independent pair was prepared. Averaging the largest signal acceptance probabilities allowed by these bounds controls the normalized trace distance in the convex-split lemma. A second bound gives a sufficient number of systems by minimizing the hypothesis-testing relative entropy over the state of the reference. Both bounds hold for density operators on separable Hilbert spaces. Comparing two distributions for the location of the hidden system gives one-shot bounds for private communication and one-way secret key distillation, including the public information available to an eavesdropper. For a fixed finite-alphabet model with separable quantum outputs and positive information advantage and variances, we recover the known Gaussian corrections to the attainable number of private or key bits from $n$ independent repetitions and bound the remaining loss by $\log_2 n+O(1)$ at fixed errors. The position-based key distillation protocol attains this bound with $O(n)$ public bits.

title: Remote Use of Quantum Machines in the Adversarial Scenario
authors: Mir Alimuddin, Leonardo Zambrano, Antonio Ac\'in
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25504v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Networked quantum technologies allow users to operate quantum machines hosted by remote servers, but classical commands alone cannot ensure that only the intended user can prepare the useful inputs that activate them. We formulate the problem of adversarial remote use of quantum machines in the framework of quantum resource theories. A device controlled by Bob is correlated to a remote user, Alice, through a bipartite state, and also to an adversary Eve holding its purification. Alice and Eve compete to programme Bob's machine by remotely preparing its inputs: the conditional state carries the quantum resource, while the measurement outcome selects the machine operation. Remote use is truly advantageous when Alice is guaranteed to unlock a larger average task value than the adversary Eve, given the same marginal state of Bob. We show that for tasks with a convex figure of merit, the competition is governed by complementary upper roofs and, for spectral tasks, where the figure of merit is invariant under unitary operations, by a corresponding entanglement imbalance. Purification, work extraction, quantum batteries, and coherence distillation show that the same noisy state may secure exclusivity one machine but not another. Finally, we order Alice's and Eve's complete programming powers through a task-independent simulation preorder, based on the ensembles each party can prepare on Bob's side. Shared quantum correlations thereby become a key resource for controlling access to remote quantum machines.

title: The computational complexity of bosonic Lindbladian fixed points
authors: En-Jui Kuo, Arsalan Motamedi, Mohammad Hafezi, Saeed Mehraban
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25519v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study the computational complexity of estimating observables and sampling from stationary states, or fixed points, of bosonic Lindbladian dynamics with bounded-degree polynomial interactions. While the complexity of transient bosonic dynamics has been investigated, understanding the computational power of bosonic fixed points requires addressing subtleties of infinite-dimensional systems, including the existence, uniqueness, and convergence of stationary states.
  We establish a broad complexity landscape spanning universal quantum computation, efficient classical simulation, sampling hardness, and undecidability. First, we show that universal quantum computation can be embedded into observable estimation at the unique fixed point of a bosonic Lindbladian with a Hamiltonian of degree at most twelve and only linear photon loss. Moreover, this fixed point can be prepared from vacuum in polynomial time. On the classical side, we identify Gaussian regimes with incoherent pumping that admit efficient photon-number sampling and establish stability of classical approximability under sufficiently weak non-Gaussian Kerr perturbations. Conversely, for Gaussian fixed points without incoherent pumping, we establish hardness of exact sampling under constant-rate linear loss and hardness of approximate sampling at inverse-polynomial loss rates under standard boson-sampling conjectures. We also relate sampling from non-Gaussian fixed points to variants of boson sampling. Finally, we prove that deciding the existence of a stationary density operator is $\mathsf{RE}$-hard, even for purely dissipative Lindbladians with degree-five jump operators acting on at most four modes.

title: High-fidelity six-dimensional optical data storage
authors: Jichao Gao, Tong Jin, Chenqi Yi, Yihui Fu, Zhi Yan, Xiya Xie, Rokas Drevinskas, Zhexiang Xiao, Lei Wang, Guangda Niu, Jingyu Zhang, Hong-Bo Sun
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25545v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Multi-dimensional optical data storage, wherein each voxel encodes multiple bits of information within a three-dimensional isotropic medium, presents a revolutionary approach to dense data storage. This approach exploits multiple degrees of freedom of light, such as intensity, polarization and wavelength, to selectively control distinct optical responses in the medium. However, increasing dimensionality exacerbates crosstalk between different encoding dimensions, thereby compromising recording fidelity. In this study, we introduce a novel six-dimensional (6D) multiplexing approach that exploits ultrafast interactions of polarized light with a three-dimensional medium. By manipulating three light parameters within a Poincar\'e-like semi-sphere, we systematically induce three distinct material responses in laser-induced nanostructures, each corresponding to a unique physical quantity: fluorescence, phase retardance, and slow axis orientation. Thanks to such multiple one-to-one correspondence between light parameters and material responses, we achieve unprecedented high fidelity, attaining a raw accuracy of 99.45%. Furthermore, this independently controlled 6D multiplexing technique maximizes the effective user capacity to 0.38 petabits per disc. The versatility of laser-induced nanostructures across multiple physical dimensions enables diverse applications, ranging from high-capacity data storage to microfluidics, optical elements, integrated photonics, micromechanics, and quantum technologies.

title: Direct measurement of the on-shot focal-spot size of a kilojoule-class petawatt laser
authors: Ryunosuke Takizawa, Keisuke Takahashi, Yuhei Kawakami, Hiroki Matsubara, Yuga Karaki, Rinya Akematsu, Ryou Oomura, Kai Kimura, Yuki Tamaru, Yasunobu Arikawa, Koji Tsubakimoto, Shinsuke Fujioka
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25552v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We report a direct, on-shot determination of the focal-spot size of a kilojoule-class, four-beam petawatt laser. Encircled-energy curves were inferred from the energy transmitted around aluminum-coated spheres of varying diameters placed at the focal plane. The 50% encircled-energy diameter D50 of each beam was obtained by fitting a two-component Gaussian mixture with Bayesian inference. With all deformable mirrors optimized in closed loop, the best-corrected alignment beam reached D50 = 34 (+4/-5) um, three times the diffraction limit of 10 um. Under full-power conditions, the thermal distortion of the main amplifier broadened this beam to D50 = 102 (+9/-8) um and reduced its peak intensity ninefold, to 2.2 (+0.6/-0.9) x 10^18 W/cm^2 at 250 J and 1.3 ps. The energy fraction of the narrow component decreased from 68% to 38%. These reference values serve facility users, and a deformable mirror upstream of the pulse compressor, now on one beam only, doubles the on-shot peak intensity.

title: A Heterogeneous CPU-GPU Framework for Finite Element Micromagnetic Simulations on Tetrahedral Meshes
authors: Zekai Zheng, Zixuan Cui, Guanghui Hu
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25565v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The design of magnetic storage materials relies on repeated micromagnetic simulations. Within each simulation, the demagnetization field evaluation and the sparse linear solve are executed at every time step and together dominate the computational cost. To address these bottlenecks, we develop a heterogeneous CPU-GPU framework that exploits the complementary computational capabilities of the two processors. In the existing AFEMAG solver, developed by Yang et al [J. Comput. Phys. 431 (2021) 110142], computationally intensive boundary integral evaluations and sparse linear solves limit performance. We offload these operations to the GPU while retaining assembly and iteration control on the CPU. We validate the framework using cases from all five $\mu$Mag standard problems, covering quasistatic hysteresis, equilibrium configurations, field-driven dynamics, and spin-transfer-torque dynamics. This approach accelerates simulations across the benchmark suite; notably, for Standard Problem 3 on a mesh of 137,313 nodes, augmenting the CPU with one NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a $17.1\times$ speedup over the CPU-only configuration. The heterogeneous AFEMAG framework thus provides an efficient and practical platform for micromagnetic simulations in the design of magnetic storage materials.

title: Algorithmic Quantum Sensing
authors: Ishaan Kannan, Aditi Venkatesh, Jordan Cotler
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25572v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We introduce a unified framework for sensing time-dependent fields through the lens of classical and quantum algorithms. First, we develop three pulse sequence protocols, namely randomized, matched, and pooled spectroscopy, which outperform established approaches such as dynamical decoupling across a wide range of tasks. These protocols attain the optimal sensitivity for linear and nonlinear AC sensing on conventional spin or qubit platforms, improving existing devices by changing only their pulse sequences. We then introduce quantum computational spectroscopy (QCS), which couples quantum sensors to a quantum processor. QCS combines two new primitives: a quantum computational frequency comb that coherently converts any classical signal into a quantum oracle, and a family of quantum algorithms that use the oracle to extract signal information in superposition. Variations can be implemented on current platforms with only one memory ancilla. We show that the ultimate limit imposed by quantum mechanics lies polynomially beyond the Heisenberg limit, and that QCS achieves it. Attaining this new limit requires quantum computation, establishing a fundamental separation between conventional and quantum computational sensing. Moreover, QCS retains beyond-Heisenberg scaling for broadband signals under constant-strength sensor depolarization, while we prove that the same noise limits any protocol lacking quantum computation to standard-quantum-limit scaling. Our result provides the first asymptotic, beyond-quadratic quantum advantage in AC metrology when noise is aligned with the signal, proving that Lindblad span conditions do not apply to broadband quantum sensing. Our work builds an algorithmic theory for designing sensing protocols and establishes quantum sensing as a new frontier for quantum algorithms, with quantum advantages that surpass the Heisenberg limit and that persist under noise.

title: Syndrome-based Calibration Using Gate-Error Amplification
authors: Andrew T. Kamen, Arielle Sanford, Frederic T. Chong, Andy J. Goldschmidt, Siddharth Dangwal
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25579v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We present Gate-Error Amplification for Recalibration with Syndromes (GEARS), a runtime calibration framework that uses gate-error amplification to efficiently tune control parameters during quantum error correction. Maintaining reliable control of large qubit arrays throughout hours-long computations requires repeated calibration to compensate for hardware drift. In conventional calibration, targeted qubits are temporarily removed from the code, introducing non-negligible space-time overhead. An elegant alternative uses syndrome information already collected during error correction as feedback for in situ recalibration, but acquiring signal requires sufficient (1) measurement budget or (2) probe strength, i.e., the size of deliberate control perturbations. More measurements improve statistical precision but result in slower control updates, while stronger perturbations produce larger calibration signals at the cost of additional errors. GEARS augments syndrome-based calibration with an established gate characterization technique called gate-error amplification. Our approach repeats selected CZ gates and probes their controls in spatially separated groups, strengthening local calibration signals while limiting the logical cost of probing. Surface code simulations show that GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces measurement requirements by approximately a factor of eight at matched gradient SNR and fixed probe strength. In closed-loop calibration, GEARS with depth-three amplification reduces excess expected logical failures by approximately 31-40% relative to calibration without amplification across the evaluated execution windows. Under time-dependent drift, GEARS increases the estimated critical drift frequency by approximately 1.9x. These results indicate that deliberately amplifying gate errors during operation can improve the long-time performance of quantum computations.

title: Seamless Gradient Pixels for Multidimensional Optical Information Interrogation
authors: Zhenchao Liu, Bochang Wu, Houxin Fan, Tingbiao Guo, Hongtao Wang, Lei Chen, Cheng-Feng Pan, Shutao Zhang, Md Abdur Rahman, Wen Siang Lew, Hongyoon Kim, Heechang Yun, Junsuk Rho, Joel K. W. Yang
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25598v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Information from light interaction with its environment can be extracted from its numerous properties. Yet capturing and interpreting this information within a single and compact platform remains challenging because conventional systems rely on discrete components and detection channels. Here we introduce the concept of "gradient pixels" that provides a universal metasurface platform to interrogate optical field information in the infrared (IR) spectrum. By continuously varying a design parameter across two dimensions, we encode multidimensional optical information into measurable spatial patterns, e.g., both spectral and polarization information are acquired from a single snapshot image. A free-form gradient pixel further enables prescribed wavelength-selective spatial patterns within a single metasurface through tailored gradient profiles. Unlike isolated filter arrays, seamless gradient-pixels multiplex neighbouring meta-atoms, increasing channel spatial density and relaxing Q-factor constraints. A 250-$\mu$m footprint of these meta-atoms achieves spectral resolution better than 100-pm over a 100-nm spectral span based on a serpentine configuration. Snapshot wavelength-polarization reconstruction yields polarization angular accuracy at 0.3$^\circ$. We extend this concept to perform near-field refractive index sensing at video rates using the same explicit parameter-space mapping. By linking far-field detection and near-field sensing, it enables spatially resolved analysis of optical fields and local dielectric environments through a common image-based readout. It offers prospects for multidimensional optical sensing, computational imaging and intelligent information processing.

title: A branch-free three-dimensional ghost-cell immersed boundary method with direction-averaged extrapolation kernels
authors: Itsuki Takarabe, Ryuto Saeki, Koji Fukagata
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25618v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Ghost-cell immersed boundary methods impose the wall boundary condition on a Cartesian grid by assigning values to the grid points just inside the body, the ghost points. A common approach reconstructs the ghost value from an image point, which requires a wall normal for every ghost point. Special treatments are also often required where the interpolation stencil leaves the fluid region, e.g., near thin, concave or highly curved parts of complex bodies. We present a ghost-cell method that needs neither wall normals nor image points. Instead of a single extrapolation direction, the method uses all fluid nodes within 2.5 grid spacings of a ghost point that satisfy a simple geometric condition. The ghost value is obtained as the average of one-dimensional linear extrapolations from these nodes through the wall crossings of the connecting segments. The weights depend only on the geometry and are computed offline as one kernel on a $5 \times 5 \times 5$ stencil per ghost point. The boundary treatment at run time is thus an explicit, branch-free weighted sum. For the flows around a sphere and the Stanford Bunny, a self-convergence study shows approximately second-order convergence of the velocity in the $L_1$ and $L_2$ norms. The maximum difference also decreases at second order for the sphere but more slowly for the Stanford Bunny, where it is observed at a few nodes next to the wall. The drag coefficient of the sphere at Reynolds numbers of 25--200 agrees with a previous study within 2.4% for 32 grid cells per diameter and 0.4% for 64. For the Stanford Bunny at a Reynolds number of 100, the force coefficients agree with a body-fitted solution within 1% for 64 grid cells per reference length, without any geometry-specific treatment. Although no pressure condition is imposed on the wall, the pressure field is smooth and consistent with the body-fitted solution.

title: Real-Time Single-Pixel Imaging via Exploiting Temporal Mixing: A Unified Calibration and Composite Readout Framework
authors: Jing-Sen Li, En-Rui Zhang, Kan-Xu Jia, Yi-Zhu Zhang, Qian-Qian Bao, Shao-Ying Meng, Xi-Hao Chen
abstract:
arXiv:2611.25700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: In high-speed optical measurements and computational imaging such as in single-pixel imaging temporal mixing arising from the mismatch between modulation and the electro-optical acquisition chain is conventionally treated as an unmitigated distortion that corrupts measurement orthogonality, breaks compressive sensing priors, fundamentally limits imaging speed, and induces catastrophic reconstruction failure. Here, we establish a transferable, unified calibration and composite-readout framework for single-pixel imaging that systematically repurposes temporal memory from a readout limitation into a powerful measurement resource. Beyond achieving robust high-fidelity recovery, this engineered approach enables cost effective, lower bandwidth configurations to consistently deliver superior image quality compared to higher bandwidth reference setups across diverse operating conditions turning a historical hardware bottleneck into an active imaging advantage. Specifically, target scenes are reconstructed directly from mixed observations without the need to recover individual pattern projections, thereby significantly advancing high-speed and video-rate single-pixel imaging capabilities. Crucially, the transferability of our framework allows calibration routines established on one hardware platform (such as digital micromirror device-based setups) to be readily transferred across different optical systems (such as rotating coding disks), paving the way for calibrated temporal memory as a versatile and generalized measurement paradigm for broader computational imaging.
